title: Norway Loses Its World Juniors Spot to Russia, but the Story Isn't Over
summary:
Norway's young hockey players may have lost their place at the world junior championships before the tournament even starts. The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said on Sunday that it has been told Norway is being bumped so Russia can take part instead.

The switch follows a recent ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which reinstated Russian hockey teams to international competition, starting with the world juniors. The tournament for the best male players under 20 opens in Alberta, Canada, on December 26, with ten nations taking part.

But the decision has not been formally announced by the International Ice Hockey Federation, and its website still lists Norway as a participant. Norway, ranked tenth going into the tournament, said it was moved down to the 1A Division to open the spot for Russia.

Russia is not guaranteed to play, either. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said he will bar the Russian team from entering Canada, which could leave the door open for Norway after all.

'The situation is still unclear,' said Norway's ice hockey secretary general, Peter Salsten. 'This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada.'

There are more complications. Six nations, including Norway, have vowed to boycott games against Russia as long as the war in Ukraine continues. Several longtime sponsors have also said they will drop out if Russia plays.

Russia has not competed in the tournament since finishing fourth in 2021. Its teams were banned after the country invaded Ukraine in February 2022. Norway said it understands that the court ruling has tied the IIHF's hands, but Salsten added that the situation 'clearly shows all the practical challenges and immediate consequences for everyone involved when countries are reinstated immediately.'
why_it_matters: Sport and world events are connected: this story shows how a war far away can change who gets to play in a youth tournament, and how countries and sponsors use their choices to take a stand.
